The Lean proof, step by step

A reader’s guide to the machine-checked proof that a locally minimal oriented bounding box has at least three edge–face contacts (Conjecture 7.1 of J. Jylänki, An Exact Algorithm for Finding Minimum Oriented Bounding Boxes, 2015). Every grey box is copied verbatim from the Lean sources. Under each one is a plain reading, and fold-out notes on what the statement says precisely — and what it does not say.

Companions: proof.html is the mathematical writeup with interactive figures; lean/README.md lists the files and how to build them. No knowledge of Lean is assumed here; section 2 explains the notation.

1. What “machine-checked” gives you

The project in lean/ is about 2,000 lines of Lean 4 built on the Mathlib library. Lean’s kernel has checked every inference in it. So the proofs do not have to be read to be trusted — if a step were wrong, the file would not compile.

What does have to be read is the statement: the handful of definitions and the final theorem. Lean guarantees that the theorem follows from the definitions; it cannot know whether boxVolume means what you mean by “the volume of the bounding box”. That part is short, and it is section 3 of this page. The rest of the page is there for understanding, not for trust.

What could still be wrong?
  • A definition that misses the intended notion. Section 3 goes through each definition and lists what to check.
  • Hypotheses that are stronger than they look, so that the theorem covers fewer boxes than you think. There are three: R is a rotation, the box has positive volume, and R is a local minimum. The last theorem of the project (exists_minimal_box_with_three_contacts, step 8) shows they can all hold at once for every point set that is not flat.
  • A fault in Lean itself. The theorems rest on the three axioms that nearly all of Mathlib uses (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) and on nothing else; in particular there is no sorry, Lean’s placeholder for a missing proof.
How to re-check it yourself

In lean/, with ~/.elan/bin on the PATH:

The second command should report exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] for each theorem.

2. Reading Lean: the notation used here

A Lean statement has the shape theorem name (h₁ : A) (h₂ : B) : C, read “if A and B, then C”. The names h₁, h₂ are labels by which the proof refers to the hypotheses. Variables in curly braces, such as {α β : ℝ}, are ordinary variables that Lean fills in by itself when the theorem is used.

LeanMeaning
Fin 3 → ℝA vector of ℝ³: a function from the index set {0, 1, 2} to the reals. x i is its i-th coordinate. Function application is written without brackets. (In Count.lean this type is abbreviated V3.)
x ⬝ᵥ uDot product x·u.
Finset (Fin 3 → ℝ)A finite set of points of ℝ³. E.card is the number of its elements.
Matrix (Fin 3) (Fin 3) ℝA real 3×3 matrix. R a m is the entry in row a, column m; Rᵀ the transpose; R.det the determinant; R *ᵥ v matrix times vector.
e mThe m-th standard basis vector (a definition of this project).
∏ m, f mThe product f 0 * f 1 * f 2.
∀ y ∈ K, …   ∃ x ∈ K, …For all / there exists a point of K.
∧   ∨   ¬   →And, or, not, implies.
False as a conclusionThe hypotheses contradict each other. A lemma “… : False” says that the situation described by its hypotheses cannot occur.
∀ᶠ s in 𝓝 (0 : ℝ), P s“P(s) holds for all s close enough to 0”: there is some ε > 0 such that P(s) holds whenever |s| < ε. Read ∀ᶠ as “eventually”. The ε is never computed.
𝓝[>] 0: only small positive s.  𝓝[≠] 0: small non-zero s.  𝓝[SO3] R: rotations close to R.
IsLocalMinOn f S af a ≤ f x for all x in the set S that are close enough to a.
IsMinOn f S af a ≤ f x for all x in S.
Collinear ℝ SAll points of S lie on one line. (Also true when S is empty or a single point.)
Fin 3 × BoolA pair (axis index, true/false). The six box faces are labelled this way.
fun x => …The function sending x to …
The proof commands (“tactics”) that appear in the annotated proofs
TacticWhat it does
intro hAssume the hypothesis of an implication (or of a negation) and call it h.
have name : P := …Prove an intermediate fact P and give it a name.
obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := hh says “there is an x with …”, or is a conjunction: take it apart and name the pieces.
rcases h with a | bh is an “or”: treat the two cases one after the other.
by_cases, by_contraCase distinction on a statement and its negation; proof by contradiction.
refine …, exact …Supply the proof, possibly with holes ?_ that become the next goals.
rw [eq], simp, unfoldRewrite with an equation; simplify with a library of rewrite rules; replace a defined name by its definition.
ringProves a polynomial identity by bringing both sides to a normal form.
field_simpClears denominators (it must be able to see that they are non-zero).
linarith [facts]Proves a linear inequality by finding a combination of the known inequalities, and of the extra facts in brackets, that adds up to it.
nlinarith [facts]The same, after also multiplying pairs of known facts with each other.
linear_combination c₁ * h₁ + c₂ * h₂Proves an equation by checking (with ring) that it is exactly that combination of the equations h₁, h₂.
positivityProves that an expression is positive or non-negative from its shape (squares, sums of positives …).
filter_upwards [h₁, h₂] with s a bTo prove “for all small s, P” from two facts of the same kind: take one s at which both hold (as a and b) and prove P there.
fun_propProves continuity of an expression built from continuous pieces.
decideSettles a finite question (here: about the three axis labels) by checking all cases.

3. The statement

This is the part to read critically. It consists of the definition of the box volume, of what a contact is, and of the theorem.

3.1 The polyhedron and its bounding boxes

In words. The polyhedron is given by a finite set K of points. supp K u is how far K reaches in direction u; width K u is its extent between the two supporting planes perpendicular to u. A box orientation is a matrix R whose columns are the three box axes, and boxVolume K R is the product of the three widths along them: the volume of the smallest box with that orientation that contains K.
How to read this precisely
  • K is a set of points, not a solid. That loses nothing: a box contains the points exactly when it contains their convex hull, and the support function of the hull is the same. Extra points inside the hull, or in the middle of an edge, change nothing.
  • K.sup' h (fun x => x ⬝ᵥ u) is the largest value of x·u over the points x of K. The if … else 0 is only there to define something for the empty set, which never occurs under the hypotheses of the theorems.
  • axis R m is the m-th column of R: the vector whose a-th coordinate is the entry R a m.
  • The number is a box volume only for orthonormal columns. boxVolume K R is defined for every matrix, but it means “volume of a box” only when the columns are perpendicular unit vectors. That is why every theorem assumes R ∈ SO3.
  • Only tight boxes are considered — one box per orientation. Nothing is lost: a box of minimal volume around K, even only locally minimal among all circumscribing boxes, must be tight, since otherwise it could be shrunk without turning it.
In words. The rotations: matrices with orthonormal columns and determinant 1.
How to read this precisely
  • It is the usual rotation group. The set is written out so that nothing is hidden behind a library name; the lemma mem_SO3_iff in Main.lean proves it equals Mathlib’s Matrix.specialOrthogonalGroup (Fin 3) ℝ.
  • Determinant +1 loses no boxes. A frame with determinant −1 becomes a rotation when one axis is reversed, and reversing an axis does not change the box.
  • Several rotations describe the same box (relabelling the axes). That is harmless for a statement about local minima.
  • “Close” means close entry by entry — the ordinary topology on 3×3 matrices.

3.2 Contacts

In words. contactSet K u collects the points of K that are highest in direction u: the points lying in the box face with outward normal u. The six faces are labelled by an axis m and a sign. A face “has an edge” when at least two points of K lie in it, and “has a face” when three of them are not on a line.
How to read this precisely
  • The contact set lists vertices; the actual contact region is their convex hull. One point: the face touches at a vertex. Several points on a line: an edge of the polyhedron lies in the face. Points not on a line: a polygonal face of the polyhedron is flush with the box face.
  • K.filter (fun x => ∀ y ∈ K, y ⬝ᵥ u ≤ x ⬝ᵥ u) keeps those x of K for which no point of K is higher along u.
  • Face labels. (m, true) is the face with outward normal +R em, (m, false) the opposite one. In f : Fin 3 × Bool, f.1 is the axis and f.2 the sign. Two faces are opposite or equal when their axes agree, and adjacent when they differ.
  • HasEdge means “at least an edge”. A face flush with a polygon also satisfies it.
In words. An edge is represented by the points of K on it. IsEdge K E says that E is exactly the set of points of K that are highest in some direction, that there are at least two of them, and that they lie on a line. IsContact K R f E says that E is such an edge and that all its points lie in the box face f.
How to read this precisely
  • “Highest in some direction” is what makes it an edge and not just two vertices. The first clause, ∃ v, E = contactSet K v, says E is a face of the polyhedron in the convex-geometry sense: the place where some supporting plane touches it. A one-dimensional face is an edge. Two opposite corners of a quadrilateral face, for instance, are not a contact set of any direction.
  • E is the whole edge. Because E must equal a contact set, it contains every point of K on that edge, so two different sets E are two different edges.
  • Containment of the points is containment of the segment. E ⊆ contactSet K (faceNormal R f) puts the points of the edge in the supporting plane of the box face; the segment between them is then in the box face too.
  • V3 is the abbreviation for Fin 3 → ℝ used in this file.

3.3 The theorem

In words. Take any finite point set K and any rotation R. If the box with orientation R has positive volume and no nearby orientation gives a smaller box, then there are three box faces f₁, f₂, f₃ and three polyhedron edges E₁, E₂, E₃ such that each edge lies in its face, the three (face, edge) pairs are different, and f₁ and f₂ are on different axes.
How to read this precisely
  • “Local minimum” is the weak notion. IsLocalMinOn (boxVolume K) SO3 R says boxVolume K R ≤ boxVolume K Q for every rotation Q close to R. Strict minima, plateaus and the global minimum are all covered.
  • “Distinct contacts” means distinct (face, edge) pairs. The three contacts need not involve three different edges or three different faces:
    • one edge lying along a box edge is in two faces and counts as two contacts;
    • a box face flush with a polygonal face supplies three or more on its own.
  • “Adjacent” is stated as f₁.1 ≠ f₂.1: the first two contacts are on faces of different axes, and two faces of a box on different axes share a box edge.
  • Positive volume is required (0 < boxVolume K R). A point set lying in a plane is excluded; it also follows that K is not empty.
  • “At least”, not “exactly”. The theorem produces three contacts; there may be more.
  • It is a necessary condition only. A box with three contacts need not be a local minimum.

Three companion statements say the same thing in other forms.

In words. ThreeContacts K R expresses the conclusion through contact sets instead of named edges: two faces on different axes each contain an edge, and either some face is flush with a polygon or three different faces each contain an edge. three_contacts proves it at every local minimum; three_contacts_of_isMinOn is the special case of a global minimum, which is Conjecture 7.1 as stated in the paper.
How the two forms are related
  • three_contacts is what the geometric argument proves. It never mentions edges of the polyhedron as objects, only how many points of K each box face contains.
  • The step to named edges is polygon geometry. If three faces each contain an edge, that is three contacts. If instead one face is flush with a polygon, one needs to know that a polygon has at least three edges and that they are edges of the polyhedron. That is proved in step 7.
  • IsMinOn implies IsLocalMinOn, so the global statement is a one-line corollary.
In words. If K has positive width in every direction, then a box of minimal volume exists, and it has three distinct edge–face contacts, two of them on adjacent faces.
How to read this precisely
  • hK : ∀ u : V3, u ≠ 0 → 0 < width K u says K is not contained in a plane: whatever direction you look along, the set has some thickness.
  • This is the statement without any “if a minimum exists”. The existence of the minimal box is part of the conclusion.

4. Map of the proof

The proof is by contradiction, in the frame of the box. Suppose a locally minimal box has too few contacts. Then the box can be moved in a way that keeps every contact it has. During such a motion the same vertices keep supporting the six faces, so the volume is an explicit algebraic function of the motion parameter — and one checks that this function strictly decreases. That contradicts minimality.

Two motions suffice: a rotation about a box axis (motion A), and a curve that keeps two edges flush (motion B). The tree shows which lemma uses which.

  • three_edge_face_contacts Count.lean — the literal statement
    • three_contacts Main.lean — contact-set form, any orientation
      • isLocalMinOn_image, boxVolume_image — rewrite everything in the box’s own coordinates (step 6)
      • three_contacts_one — the theorem in the box frame; the case analysis (step 5)
        • caseA Cases.lean — motion A shrinks the box (step 3)
          • plane_rotation — what local minimality says for a rotation about an axis
        • caseB Cases.lean — motion B shrinks the box (step 4)
          • plane_rotation, first_order_bounds — torque balance, two of three entries
          • caseB_algebra Algebra.lean — the rest, as a statement about real numbers
            • first_order_p — torque balance, third entry
            • sq_le_one_of_abs — the bound |p|, |q|, |r| ≤ 1
            • quartic_core — the volume strictly decreases
              • polyA_sub_polyB, c2_eq_hess, hess_nonpos, diag_of_hess_eq_zero
        • both motions rest on Motion.lean: eventually_width_eq (step 1) and frame_eventually (step 2)
    • three_edges_of_face Count.lean — a flush polygon contributes three edges (step 7)
      • contactSet_contactSet, three_edges_planar, two_edges_at_lexmin
  • exists_minimal_box_with_three_contacts Count.lean

Three steps are carried out differently from the writeup, because they are easier to formalize. Curves of rotations are explicit frames with polynomial entries instead of exp([ω]×). The torque balance comes from three one-parameter motions instead of a separating hyperplane. The diagonal case is an exact identity instead of AM–GM. Each is pointed out below where it occurs.

5. Step 1: contacts persist under small motions

When a box face is tilted slightly, which vertex supports it afterwards? One of those that touched it before.

In words. Let N(s) be a direction that depends continuously on s and equals u at s = 0. Then for all s close to 0, the point of K that reaches farthest in direction N(s) can be taken from the contact set of u.
How to read this precisely
  • N : ℝ → Fin 3 → ℝ is a curve of vectors: N s is the direction at parameter s. It need not have unit length.
  • ContinuousAt N 0 and N 0 = u are the only assumptions on the curve.
  • The conclusion is an “eventually” statement. It holds for |s| below some ε that depends on K and on the curve. Nothing is claimed for larger s.
  • Which contact vertex y it is may depend on s. If the face contained an edge and is tilted about a line across that edge, it is one endpoint for s > 0 and the other for s < 0.
Why it is true

K is finite. At s = 0 every point outside the contact set is lower than the contact points by a positive gap. Heights depend continuously on s, so each such point stays lower for small s; and finitely many “for small s” statements hold simultaneously. In Lean the last remark is the lemma Filter.eventually_all_finset.

In words. Suppose that for every s all contact points of the face u have the same height along N(s) as a fixed point P, and all contact points of the opposite face the same height as Q. Then for small s the width along N(s) is the chord (P − Q)·N(s).
How to read this precisely
  • The two hypotheses say “both faces keep their contact sets”. If the tilted plane still passes through all the old contact vertices, they are all still highest, and any one of them measures the height.
  • When do they hold? Trivially if the face touches a single vertex. If it contains an edge with direction a, they hold when N(s) stays perpendicular to a.
  • This is “F = G on M” of the writeup: along a motion that keeps the contacts, the true width equals the width between two fixed points.
  • The hypotheses are for all s, the conclusion only for small s. Far from 0 other vertices may take over.

6. Step 2: local minimality along a motion

The hypothesis “R is a local minimum” is about all rotations near R. To use it one has to exhibit particular nearby rotations. This lemma turns any moving orthogonal frame into such a family and states what minimality says about it.

In words. Let N(s)₀, N(s)₁, N(s)₂ be three vectors that are pairwise perpendicular for every s, depend continuously on s, and are the standard basis at s = 0. If the identity orientation is a local minimum, then for small s
(volume at s = 0) · |N₀| · |N₁| · |N₂|  ≤  width(N₀) · width(N₁) · width(N₂).
How to read this precisely
  • N s m is the m-th frame vector at parameter s; √(N s m ⬝ᵥ N s m) is its length.
  • The vectors are not unit vectors, on purpose. This lets their coordinates be polynomials in s. The box with axes along them has volume ∏ width(Nm) / |Nm|; the inequality is “that volume is at least the starting volume” with the lengths multiplied over.
  • The orientation is 1, the identity matrix. This lemma lives in the frame of the box; step 6 shows that this is no restriction.
  • There is no right-handedness hypothesis. It is not needed: see the next note.
  • In the box frame this is the only place where the local-minimum hypothesis is used. Everything else is geometry of the motion and algebra.
Why it is true

Divide each vector by its length; the three unit vectors are the columns of a matrix Q(s) with orthonormal columns, and Q(s) → 1 as s → 0. Its determinant is ±1, depends continuously on s and is 1 at s = 0, so it is 1 for small s: the matrix is a rotation near the identity. Local minimality gives boxVolume K 1 ≤ boxVolume K (Q s), and width(N/|N|) = width(N)/|N| turns that into the displayed inequality.

The variant frame_eventually3 states the same for three curves attached to three distinct axis labels i, j, k, so that later lemmas hold for every choice of axes without repeating the argument.

7. Step 3: motion A, rotation about a box axis

Turn the box about its axis ei. Written with s = tan(angle), the other two axes become ej − s ek and ek + s ej, each of length √(1 + s²).

In words. Assume the two faces of axis k keep their contact points Pk, Qk under this rotation. Then for every small s there is a pair of contact vertices P, Q of the faces ±ej with
wj wk (1 + s²)  ≤  (wj − s·(P − Q)k) · (wk + s·(Pk − Qk)j).
How to read this precisely
  • i, j, k are any three different axis labels (hij, hik, hjk). One proof covers all six arrangements.
  • The right-hand side is the product of the two new widths; the left-hand side is the old product times the two new lengths. The width along the rotation axis does not change and has been cancelled, which is what hwi : 0 < width K (e i) is needed for.
  • hkp, hkm: every contact point of the face +ek (resp. −ek) has the same j-coordinate as Pk (resp. Qk). So that face touches a single vertex, or an edge parallel to the rotation axis.
  • Nothing is assumed about the faces ±ej. That is why the pair P, Q sits inside the “for all small s”: it may be a different pair for different s.
In words. If each of the four faces of the axes j and k touches the polyhedron in a single vertex or along an edge parallel to ei, the box is not a local minimum: turning it about ei makes it smaller.
How to read this precisely
  • The conclusion is False. The lemma says its hypotheses cannot all hold; since one of them is hmin, it says: a box in this configuration is not a local minimum.
  • hkp: any two contact points of the face +ek have equal j-coordinates. They have equal k-coordinates anyway, so they differ only along ei. The other three hypotheses say the same for the other three faces.
  • The two faces of axis i are unrestricted. They may contain edges or whole polygons. So the lemma covers “no contacts at all”, “all contacts on one pair of opposite faces”, and more.
  • No bound on the contact ratios is needed here — unlike motion B.
Why it is true

Now all four faces keep their contact points, so the pair P, Q in plane_rotation is fixed. Write f = (Pj − Qj)k and g = (Pk − Qk)j. Expanding the inequality gives, for all small s of either sign,

0  ≤  s·(wj g − f wk) − s²·(f g + wj wk).
  1. Because s can be positive or negative, the coefficient of s must vanish: wj g = f wk.
  2. Then f g = f² wk/wj ≥ 0, so the right-hand side is −s²·(positive), which is negative for s ≠ 0.

In the writeup’s normalised variables, with x = f/wj = g/wk, the relative volume is (1 − s²x²)/(1 + s²) < 1. That is the statement H(ei) ≤ −2.

The Lean proof, annotated
  • obtain ⟨Pk, hPk⟩ := contactSet_nonempty … (four times): pick one contact vertex on each of the four faces.
  • have h := plane_rotation …: the inequality of the previous lemma, with a pair that may depend on s.
  • have h': since the faces ±ej have constant k-coordinate (hjp, hjm), the pair can be replaced by the fixed one. rwa means “rewrite, then the goal is one of the known facts”.
  • generalize … = wj etc.: forget where the four numbers came from; from here on it is a statement about reals wj, wk, f, g.
  • hfo: point 1 above, by the lemma first_order_zero (shown in step 4).
  • obtain ⟨s, hs, hs0⟩ := ….exists: from “for all small s” pick one actual s ≠ 0.
  • hfg: f g ≥ 0. The last nlinarith is point 2.

8. Step 4: motion B, the curve keeping two edges

This is the heart of the theorem: a box flush with one edge on a face of axis i and one edge on a face of axis j, touching single vertices elsewhere. No rotation about a box axis keeps both edges flush. There is a curve that does.

8.1 The lemma

In words. Use coordinates (i, j, k). If the faces of axis i touch the polyhedron at most along edges of direction (0, α, 1), those of axis j at most along edges of direction (β, 0, 1), and those of axis k in single vertices, then the box is not a local minimum.
How to read this precisely
  • hip: any two contact points y, y′ of the face +ei satisfy yj − y′j = α (yk − y′k). Their i-coordinates agree anyway, so y − y′ is a multiple of (0, α, 1). him is the same for the opposite face.
  • α and β are the slopes of the two edges, supplied by whoever uses the lemma. An edge of direction (0, 1, 0) — parallel to ej — has no such slope. That configuration is handled by motion A instead.
  • “At most”: a single vertex satisfies hip trivially. So the lemma also allows the edge to be on only one of the two opposite faces, which is the case the theorem needs.
  • It allows more than the theorem needs. Parallel edges on both faces of an axis satisfy the hypotheses too. So some boxes with four contacts are excluded as well.
  • hkp, hkm: contact points of the faces ±ek agree in their i- and j-coordinates (and in the k-coordinate anyway): each of these faces touches one vertex.

8.2 The curve

In words. lin3 i j k a b c is the vector with coordinates a, b, c along the axes i, j, k. So the moving frame is
Ni = (1, t, −αt),   Nj = (−t, 1 + αβt, βt),   Nk = Ni × Nj = (αt + β(1+α²)t², −βt + αt², 1 + αβt + t²).
How to read this precisely
  • The edges stay flush. Ni·(0, α, 1) = αt − αt = 0 and Nj·(β, 0, 1) = −βt + βt = 0 for every t: each face normal stays perpendicular to its edge.
  • The frame is orthogonal for every t. The three dot products vanish identically; in the Lean proof each is one line ending in ring.
  • Lengths. |Nk|² = |Ni|²·|Nj|², so the product of the three lengths is |Ni|²·|Nj|², a polynomial. This is polyA below.
  • This replaces the implicit function theorem of the writeup. The set of orientations keeping both edges is a curve; here it is written down, in a parametrisation chosen so that everything is polynomial in t.
  • Its direction at t = 0 is the rotation vector ω = (β, α, 1).

8.3 The volume along the curve

Along this curve all six faces keep their contact sets, so by eventually_width_eq every width is a chord dotted with a frame vector. Choose one contact point on each face and let Dm be the chord across axis m, with xm = Dm/wm. Then frame_eventually says, after dividing by the three widths: polyA ≤ polyB for small t.

In words. polyA is the product of the three frame-vector lengths. polyB is the product of the three normalised widths xm·Nm(t). The box volume at parameter t, divided by the starting volume, is polyB / polyA.
How to read this precisely
  • The parameters are the entries of the contact matrix X with rows xi = (1, p₁, q), xj = (p₂, 1, r), xk = (q, r, 1). The diagonal is 1 because a chord across axis m spans exactly the width wm.
  • p₁ and p₂ are kept separate because their equality has not been shown yet; it comes out of the next step. The other two symmetries are already built in.
  • The three factors of polyB are xi·Ni, xj·Nj, xk·Nk, multiplied out.
  • “polyA ≤ polyB for small t” is “the box does not get smaller along the curve”. The aim is to refute it.
In words. The difference is exactly a quartic in t with no constant term: its linear coefficient is p₂ − p₁, and c2, c3, c4 are explicit polynomials in α, β, p₁, p₂, q, r.
How to read this precisely
  • It is an identity, not an approximation. There is no O(t³) remainder anywhere in the formal proof.
  • The coefficients were produced by computer algebra (scripts/lean_algebra.py, with about thirty terms each for c3 and c4), but they are not trusted: the proof of this lemma is unfold polyA polyB c2 c3 c4; ring, i.e. Lean multiplies everything out and compares.

8.4 First order: the torque balance

The writeup’s Lemma 1 says the contact points can be chosen so that the matrix X is symmetric. In Lean the three symmetries are obtained one at a time, each from a one-parameter motion and this elementary fact:

In words. If c·t + t²·ρ(t) ≤ 0 for all small t of both signs, with ρ continuous at 0, then c = 0. This is the only analysis in the proof; it stands in for “the derivative vanishes at a minimum”.
In words. If the box does not get smaller along the two-edge curve, then Xij = Xji. (Apply the previous lemma to the expansion: the linear coefficient p₂ − p₁ must vanish.)
In words. This handles a rotation that breaks an edge contact. There are finitely many candidate chords τ, with transverse components δ(τ). If for every small s at least one of them satisfies the inequality of plane_rotation, then some chord has δ/wj ≤ g/wk and some chord has δ/wj ≥ g/wk.
How to read this precisely
  • How it is used. Rotate in the plane (i, k). The faces of axis k keep their vertices; the edge on axis i lifts off, and one of its endpoints becomes the supporting vertex — which one depends on the sign of s. The candidate chords are the pairs (contact vertex of +ei, contact vertex of −ei). The conclusion reads Xik(low chord) ≤ Xki ≤ Xik(high chord).
  • So Xki lies between the values of Xik at two real chords. Xik varies linearly as the contact point slides along the edge, so at some point of the edge it equals Xki exactly. That point is the contact point Pi of the writeup’s Lemma 1.
  • The Lean proof never constructs that point. It only uses “between”: a quantity between two values that fit in the box also fits in the box.
  • The inequalities are cross-multiplied (δ τ * wk ≤ g * wj) to avoid division.
  • This replaces the separating-hyperplane argument. The same is done in the plane (j, k) for Xjk = Xkj.
Why it is true

For s > 0 the factor wj − s·δ is largest for the chord with the smallest δ, so the inequality holds with that one chord for all small positive s; the one-sided version of the first-order lemma (first_order_pos) gives the first bound. For s < 0 it is the chord with the largest δ, and first_order_neg gives the second.

8.5 The bound |p|, |q|, |r| ≤ 1

In words. A number a with |a|·u ≤ v and |a|·v ≤ u satisfies a² ≤ 1.
How to read this precisely
  • With a = p, u = wi, v = wj: the chord across axis i reaches |p|·wi in the j-direction, which must fit in the width wj. The chord across axis j reaches |p|·wj in the i-direction, which must fit in wi. Both use the same p because of the torque balance.
  • “Must fit” is abs_coord_sub_le in Defs.lean: for two points of K, a coordinate difference is at most the width in that coordinate.
  • The bound is written a ^ 2 ≤ 1 instead of |a| ≤ 1. It is the same thing and easier for the arithmetic tactics.
  • This is the writeup’s Lemma 2 and its Figure 2.

8.6 Second order: the Hessian

In words. hess p q r w1 w2 w3 is the quadratic form H(ω) of the writeup at ω = (w₁, w₂, w₃). Once X is symmetric, the t² coefficient of polyA − polyB is −½H at the curve’s direction (β, α, 1). H equals minus a sum of nine terms, and when p², q², r² ≤ 1 each of them is non-negative, so H ≤ 0.
How to read this precisely
  • c2 α β p p q r: the argument p appears twice because p₁ = p₂ = p now.
  • hess_nonpos holds for every ω, not only the one needed. It is the writeup’s Lemma 3.
  • The sign. c2 = -(1/2) * hess and hess ≤ 0 give c2 ≥ 0: to second order, polyA − polyB is non-negative, i.e. the volume does not increase.
  • Six of the nine terms are squares; three are (1 − p²)·square and the like. Those three are where the bound of 8.5 enters, and the only place.
The Lean proof of hess_nonpos, annotated
  • rw [hess_eq]: replace H by minus the sum of nine terms.
  • h1, h2, h3: a product of two non-negative numbers is non-negative (mul_nonneg); the first factor is 1 − p² ≥ 0 by hp, the second is a square.
  • linarith […]: hand over the six squares as extra facts; minus a sum of nine non-negative terms is ≤ 0.

8.7 The strict decrease, including the diagonal case

In words. H vanishes at the direction (β, α, 1) only if α and β are ±1 and (p, q, r) = (αβ, β, α). This is the writeup’s “diagonal case”: the box is a cube, every chord is a space diagonal, and the curve starts in the direction of that diagonal.
In words. For a symmetric contact matrix with entries of absolute value at most 1, it is not the case that polyA ≤ polyB for all small t. Arbitrarily close to 0 there is a t with polyB < polyA: the box got smaller.
How to read this precisely
  • The statement is a negation of an “eventually”. ¬ ∀ᶠ t in 𝓝 0, A t ≤ B t says: no matter how small an interval around 0 you take, some t in it violates A ≤ B. That is exactly the negation of “local minimum along the curve”.
  • In fact every small t ≠ 0 violates it, as the proof shows; the weaker form is all that is needed.
  • α and β are unrestricted. Any two edge slopes will do.
Why it is true

By hess_nonpos, H < 0 or H = 0 at (β, α, 1).

  • H < 0. Then c2 > 0 and polyA − polyB = t²·(c2 + t·(…)). The bracket is continuous and positive at t = 0, hence positive for small t; times t² > 0 the difference is positive.
  • H = 0. Then the five equations above hold, and substituting them the difference collapses to exactly 6t⁴, positive for t ≠ 0. The writeup uses the AM–GM inequality at this point; along this particular curve the identity makes it unnecessary.
The Lean proof of quartic_core, annotated
  • intro h: to prove a negation, assume the statement — h is “A ≤ B for all small t” — and derive a contradiction.
  • hne: among the small t other than 0, all are ≠ 0. A triviality, needed later to pick a non-zero t.
  • rcases (hess_nonpos …).lt_or_eq with hlt | heq: the two cases H < 0 and H = 0.
  • First case. hc2: c2 > 0. hcont, hpos: the bracket is positive for all small t. obtain ⟨t, ⟨ht1, ht2⟩, ht0⟩ := ….exists: pick one t that is small enough for both h and hpos and is not 0. hexp: the expansion at that t. nlinarith: t² times a positive number is positive, contradicting ht1.
  • Second case. diag_of_hess_eq_zero gives the five equations. key: the difference is 6t⁴. In its proof, rw substitutes q, r, p, and linear_combination … * hα + … * hβ says: the identity is this multiple of α² = 1 plus that multiple of β² = 1. Lean checks that by expanding. The two multipliers were found by polynomial division (scripts/lean_diag.py).

8.8 Putting motion B together

In words. This lemma is the bridge between geometry and algebra. Its hypotheses are everything the geometry provides, stated as facts about real numbers; its conclusion is that they are contradictory. caseB collects these facts from the previous steps and hands them over.
How to read this precisely — what each hypothesis is
NamesMeaning
wi wj wkThe three side lengths of the box, all positive.
dij dik, dji djk, dki dkjTransverse components of one chosen chord per axis: dij is the j-component of the chord across axis i, and so on. (Its own component is the width.)
aj ak and aj' ak'The “low” and the “high” chord across axis i delivered by first_order_bounds.
h1 h1'Xik(low) ≤ Xki ≤ Xik(high), cross-multiplied.
h2 h2'These chords differ from the chosen one by a multiple of the edge direction (0, α, 1).
h3 h3' h4 h4'They fit in the box.
bi bk …, g1 … g4'The same for axis j and the edge direction (β, 0, 1).
hki hkjThe chord across axis k fits in the box.
hevLocal minimality along the two-edge curve, before normalisation: starting volume times polyA is at most the product of the three new widths.
Why it is true — the order of the argument
  1. Define q = dki/wk and r = dkj/wk, and let p₁, p₂ be the values of Xij, Xji at the points of the two edges where Xik = q and Xjk = r. Dividing hev by the widths turns it into polyA ≤ polyB.
  2. first_order_p: p₁ = p₂. The contact matrix is now symmetric.
  3. sq_le_one_of_abs, three times: p², q², r² ≤ 1. The “between” hypotheses are used here, to see that the chords through the virtual contact points still fit in the box.
  4. quartic_core: contradiction.

9. Step 5: the case analysis

In words. The theorem in the frame of the box: if the identity orientation is a local minimum with positive volume, the box has the three contacts.

The proof assumes the conclusion fails and shows that one of the two motions applies.

SituationMotionLemma
No two faces on different axes both contain an edge. (All contacts lie on one axis i, or there are none.)Rotate about ei.caseA
Exactly two faces contain an edge, on axes i ≠ j; no face is flush with a polygon. The edge on axis i is parallel to ej. Rotate about ej.caseA
The same, with the edge on axis j parallel to ei. Rotate about ei.caseA
The same, with neither edge parallel to the other face’s axis. Follow the two-edge curve.caseB
How to read this precisely
  • The first row proves the first half of ThreeContacts (two faces on different axes contain an edge). It is O’Rourke’s theorem, and Step 4 of the writeup.
  • The other rows prove the second half by contradiction. Assume no face is flush with a polygon and there are no three faces with an edge. Together with the two faces from the first half, every other face then touches a single vertex, and the two contact sets are segments.
  • “Parallel to ej” is expressed by coordinates: all contact points of that face have the same k-coordinate, k being the third axis. They share the i-coordinate anyway.
  • In the last row the slopes α, β exist because each contact set is collinear and not at constant k; that is the lemma exists_slope below.
  • The split differs slightly from the writeup’s table. There, the special row requires both edges to be parallel to the other axis. Here one is enough for a rotation about a box axis to work, which leaves a smaller generic case.
In words. If the points of S lie on a line and two of them differ in the k-coordinate, then along S the n-coordinate changes α times as fast as the k-coordinate, for some α.

10. Step 6: from the box frame to any orientation

Steps 1 to 5 took the box to be axis-aligned. For a box with orientation R, write the points in the coordinates of the box.

In words. toFrame R x are the coordinates of the point x in the frame R, and K.image (toFrame R) is the point set in those coordinates. Its box with orientation Q has the same volume as the box of K with orientation R Q. So if R is a local minimum for K, the identity is a local minimum for the transformed set, and the theorem in the box frame applies.
How to read this precisely
  • Rᵀ *ᵥ x is the vector of dot products of x with the columns of R.
  • Where R ∈ SO3 is used: multiplying by R must map rotations near the identity to rotations near R.
  • The conclusion travels back through hasEdge_of_image and hasFace_of_image: a contact of the transformed set with a face of the axis-aligned box is a contact of K with the corresponding face of the box R.

11. Step 7: counting contacts literally

three_contacts may conclude “some box face is flush with a polygon”. To turn that into three named edges one needs two facts of polygon geometry. Both are proved in Count.lean.

In words. A face of a face is a face. Tilt the supporting plane with normal u very slightly towards v: the points that remain in contact are exactly those points of the old contact set that are highest in direction v.
How to read this precisely
  • contactSet (contactSet K u) v is a contact set of the contact set: among the points of K on the face u, those highest along v. When the face is a polygon and v points out of one of its sides, this is an edge of the polygon.
  • The left-hand side is a contact set of K itself, in the direction u + εv. So that edge of the polygon is an edge of the polyhedron in the sense of IsEdge.
  • Some ε > 0 exists; its size is not given. The proof is the persistence argument of step 1 once more.
In words. A polygon has at least three edges. If the finite set S lies in a plane with normal u and its points are not all on one line, there are three directions whose contact sets within S are segments (collinear, at least two points) and are pairwise different.
How to read this precisely
  • hplane says all points of S have the same height along u: S is planar.
  • The directions v₁, v₂, v₃ are the outward normals of three sides of the polygon.
  • “Different” is about the point sets, so these are three different edges, not one edge found three times.
Why it is true

Pick two coordinates (a, b) that work as coordinates on the plane (possible because some component of u is non-zero). Let x₀ be the lexicographically smallest point of S: leftmost, and lowest among the leftmost. Look at the slopes of the lines from x₀ to the points further right.

  • The smallest slope gives a line with all of S on one side: the lower edge at x₀.
  • The largest slope gives the upper edge — unless other points share the first coordinate of x₀, in which case the vertical line through them is the upper edge.
  • The two edges are different, because otherwise all slopes would agree and S would be collinear.

That is the lemma two_edges_at_lexmin. Apply it again at the lexicographically largest point x₁ (its parameter s = -1 reverses the order). That gives four edges, two through x₀ and two through x₁. The two points are different, since otherwise S would be a single point. If only two of the four edges were different, both would pass through both x₀ and x₁; but two segment faces through the same two points coincide (contactSet_eq_of_two). So at least three are different.

The final assembly: the Lean proof of three_edge_face_contacts, annotated
  • obtain ⟨⟨f, g, hfg, hf, hg⟩, h2⟩ := three_contacts …: take ThreeContacts apart. The first half gives two faces f, g on different axes with an edge each; h2 is the “or”.
  • rcases h2 with … | …: the two alternatives.
  • First alternative: a face f0 flush with a polygon. three_edges_of_face gives edges E₁ ≠ E₂ in it. other: one of f, g is on a different axis than f0; call it g0 and take an edge Eg in it. The three contacts are (f0, E₁), (g0, Eg), (f0, E₂).
  • Second alternative: three different faces, each with an edge (exists_contact_of_hasEdge). They are ordered so that the first two are on different axes. That is always possible: if f' and g' are on the same axis they are opposite, and then the third face h' cannot be on that axis as well (bool3: a sign has only two values).
  • The remaining lines prove that the three pairs are different, from the faces or the edges being different.

12. Step 8: a minimal box exists

In words. The set of rotations is compact and the box volume depends continuously on the orientation, so the volume attains its minimum. If K is not flat, that minimum is positive, and the main theorem applies to it.
How to read this precisely
  • This makes the conjecture’s wording non-vacuous. “A box of minimal volume has …” would be empty talk if no such box existed.
  • It also shows the hypotheses of the main theorem are consistent: for every non-flat point set there is an orientation satisfying all of them.
  • Compactness is proved directly: the set is closed (it is defined by equations between continuous functions) and every entry of a rotation matrix lies in [−1, 1].

13. What the theorem does not say

  • It is necessary, not sufficient. Three contacts do not make a box a local minimum. Deciding which three-contact boxes are minima is still the job of the enumeration in the paper’s algorithm.
  • It does not say which faces or edges are involved, nor that three different edges or three different faces occur.
  • It says nothing about flat point sets (zero box volume), and nothing about bodies that are not the hull of finitely many points.
  • It is about volume. The corresponding question for minimal surface area is not addressed.
  • It gives no algorithm and no complexity bound. It justifies restricting a search to boxes with three contacts; it does not say how many there are.

Two by-products are stronger than what the theorem needs, and are stated exactly by the lemmas above: caseA excludes every box whose four faces around some axis each touch a vertex or an edge parallel to that axis, whatever happens on the remaining two faces; and caseB excludes boxes with parallel edges on both faces of two axes and single vertices on the third.
